source.title: REMEDI: A Benchmark for Retention and Unlearning Evaluation in Multi-label Clinical Disease Inference
source.authors: Anurag Sharma; Sai Teja Chunchu; Prasenjit Mitra; Sandipan Sikdar; Koustav Rudra

record.tranche_reason: Extends evaluation of machine unlearning to clinical multi-label disease classification and reports membership-inference results, but does not test the claimed knowledge-recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates unlearning of patient records and reports loss-based membership-inference (MIA) scores. MIA tests whether forget records are distinguishable from holdout records; it does not test recovery of targeted knowledge by relearning, activation edits, quantization, or prompting. MIA results are recorded as findings about a related privacy measure, not as tests of versions A–F. The paper also reports utility results, but they do not measure any of the specified recovery behaviors.
record.test_reason: The paper benchmarks instance-level unlearning of patient records in fine-tuned BERT encoder classifiers (BioLinkBERT, BioBERT). It reports macro-F1 on test, forget and retain sets and a loss-based MIA score. It applies no recovery attack after unlearning: no relearning, no activation ablation, no quantization, no prompting. It proposes no method claimed to resist such attacks. The goal is matching a retrained model, not driving targeted-knowledge accuracy to chance, so the forget-set F1 does not measure version A's effect either. WMDP and WHP appear only in related work. The record's 'tests/T3' is wrong: the study neither tests nor uses the shallow-unlearning finding.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find a utility–unlearning trade-off and judge existing methods largely unsuited to multi-label clinical tasks. They name SCRUB as having the best utility–privacy balance. They report that success on small deletions does not transfer to large forget sets. They also claim BioLinkBERT is more resilient than BioBERT. They draw no conclusions about recovery attacks.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates gradient ascent, adversarial unlearning, Bad Teacher, and SCRUB for patient-record deletion in clinical multi-label classification; it does not apply the recovery procedures in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary across BioLinkBERT and BioBERT, unlearning method, and forget-set setting/size; additional split results are said to be in the repository.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss-based MIA scores after instance-level unlearning of patient records stay low (0.01–0.12) for every method and both encoders. Unlearned models are often no closer to the retrained model than the original model is. This measures membership leakage, not recovery of hidden knowledge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In clinical encoder classifiers, loss-based membership leakage after instance-level unlearning is small and varies by method, model and forget setting.

record.problems: The reported MIA tables provide point values without uncertainty estimates. The MIA measure is limited to loss-based membership inference and does not evaluate knowledge recovery through the attacks in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: Utility F1 results for test, forget, and retain sets in Tables 2 and 3, and additional forget-size results in Figure 2, are not included: they assess clinical classification utility/forgetting rather than any of versions A–F's recovery behaviors. The text says further split results are in the repository but does not report their values here.

untested.parts: No recovery attack of any kind. Forget-set F1 is meant to match retraining, not to reach chance. Subjects are encoder classifiers forgetting patient instances, not LLMs forgetting knowledge.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of blocking versus deletion.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language or in-context recovery attack.
No method is claimed or tested to resist recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from tests/T3 to cites_only/T6. The subjects are BERT-style encoder classifiers. The task is instance-level deletion of patient records, not concept-level knowledge removal in generative LLMs, and no attack is run. Two consistency problems in the source: 'GA+' is undefined, and the GA+R/GA labels appear to differ between Tables 2 and 3. Also, the authors' claim that BioLinkBERT is consistently better on privacy is not borne out row by row: in Table 2, BioLinkBERT's MIA for GA+R is 0.11 versus BioBERT's 0.08. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test simple attacks for recovery of targeted knowledge after unlearning; its forget-set classification utility and membership-inference measures do not establish the combined claim.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of access blocking versus deletion.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery attack.
No counter-method is tested against the specified recovery attacks.
